name: Photodynamic hair removal

lead: Photodynamic hair removal uses a photosensitizing compound, applied to the skin, and a matching light source. When the light activates the compound it generates reactive oxygen that damages nearby cells, here the target being the hair follicle.
The appeal for looks is smooth, hair-free skin for people whose hair is pale or non-pigmented and so does not respond well to standard laser hair removal, which depends on pigment to absorb light.

paras: In research settings a photosensitizer precursor such as aminolevulinic acid is applied, allowed to build up in the follicle, and the area is then illuminated. This is done by clinicians or researchers rather than as an at-home routine.
Photosensitizers can make skin sensitive to light for days to weeks. Reported effects in the one animal study found were a temporary transition of hairs rather than follicle destruction.

angle.text: The idea is smoother, hair-free skin for people whose hair lacks the pigment that laser systems need. Published work so far is early-stage.

lead: Photodynamic therapy uses a photosensitizer, light of a suitable wavelength, and oxygen. The activated agent produces reactive oxygen species, mainly singlet oxygen, that damage nearby cells, and the effect stays localized to where light lands [1].

Conventional laser hair removal relies on pigment (melanin) to absorb light, which leaves white, grey or light blond hair hard to treat. Researchers have therefore explored photodynamic approaches for non-pigmented hair [2]. A 2016 animal study of this concept reported a temporary, catagen-like transformation in non-pigmented hair [2].
Wikipedia's photodynamic therapy article does not describe a hair-removal use, but notes topical aminolevulinic acid has been studied in later-phase trials for excess hair growth (hirsutism) [1].

paras: A photosensitizer such as 5-aminolaevulinic acid, which the body converts to protoporphyrin IX, concentrates in tissue and is switched on by light. The resulting reactive oxygen kills nearby cells, and damage is limited to illuminated areas [1]. Photosensitizers can cause skin photosensitivity for days to weeks, with ALA clearing faster than some others [1].

A PubMed search surfaced a 2016 Lasers in Surgery and Medicine paper by Shin and colleagues, in an animal model, on removal of non-pigmented hair with photodynamic therapy, which motivates the work by noting that non-pigmented hairs lack chromophores for lasers; the authors report a temporary catagen-like change [2]. A 2013 clinical report on PDT using porphyrin precursors describes PDT as established for some skin conditions and for hair removal in its summary [2].

No studies found of photodynamic hair removal in routine cosmetic use in people. The available work is preclinical or small experimental research, and photodynamic therapy in dermatology is otherwise approved for conditions such as actinic keratosis and some skin cancers [1].

timeline.event: Animal-model study of photodynamic removal of non-pigmented hair published [2].
